sentences.text: Last time, every clinic got a line of its own, all with the same tilt.
Alder's line sits 0.87 above Cedar's. At the lower-risk end, at the higher-risk end, anywhere you look: the same 0.87.
On the log-odds ruler, a step of 0.87 multiplies the odds by 2.4.
So in some sense, Alder is 2.4 times Cedar. But 2.4 times what?
Here are three ways to finish that sentence.
One: Alder has 2.4 times as many readmissions.
Two: at Alder, each patient is 2.4 times as likely to be readmitted.
Three: at Alder, each patient's odds of readmission are 2.4 times as high.
Only one of them is right. Pick one before we go on.
Welcome back to Model in Motion.
Today: reading gamma.
Start with the first, and count.
Alder had 13 readmissions among 30 patients. Cedar had 8 among 20. That is 43% against 40%: almost level.
And we already know why raw counts settle nothing: they depend on who each clinic treats.
The second reading: each patient is 2.4 times as likely to come back.
Take a lower-risk patient. The model gives 18% at Cedar and 34% at Alder. That is 1.9 times, not 2.4.
For a higher-risk patient, 62% becomes 80%: only 1.3 times.
And it could never be 2.4. That would be a chance of nearly 150%.
Now the third. Turn those probabilities into odds.
For the lower-risk patient: 0.22 at Cedar, 0.52 at Alder. 2.4 times.
For the higher-risk patient: 1.64 and 3.91. 2.4 times again.
That is what a gap between two gammas means. For patients who look the same on paper, one at each clinic, the odds differ by a single multiplier: the odds ratio.
Here are the two clinics as S-curves: one shape, slid sideways by that gap.
Now slide a patient along, from low risk to high, and read both curves.
A patient with a 5% chance at Cedar has 11% at Alder: 6 points more.
At 18%, where Cedar's lower-risk patients sit, Alder gives 34%: 16 points.
At 50%, it is 70%: 20 points.
At 62%, Cedar's higher-risk patients: 80%. That's 18 points.
And at 90%, 96%: back down to 6.
One gap, one odds ratio. But the difference in probability swells in the middle and fades at both ends.
The ratio of probabilities shrinks all the way: 2.2 at the low end, 1.06 at the top. Only when readmission is rare does it come close to 2.4.
So what a gap costs in readmissions depends on which patients a clinic sees.
Last time we said: read the gaps, not the gammas themselves. Here is why.
A gamma is read where every risk factor is zero. So far, zero has meant a lower-risk patient.
But that was our choice. Call the higher-risk patient zero instead.
Every gamma climbs by 2.02: the whole step.
Or put zero halfway between, at a patient who doesn't exist. Now every gamma is 1.01 above where it started.
Through all of this, no line has moved, and no patient's probability has changed.
And the gap between Alder and Cedar is 0.87 every time.
A gamma depends on where we put zero. A gap doesn't.
One warning before we finish.
Suppose all 103 patients went to Cedar. The model says 38% would come back. All of them at Alder: 55%.
Put those two rates on the log-odds ruler. They are 0.69 apart, not 0.87.
Nothing has gone wrong. The 0.87 compares one kind of patient at a time. The 0.69 compares two averages, taken over patients of very different risk.
Those are different questions, and the second gives the smaller answer whenever patients differ in risk.
So if a gap from a model looks bigger than the gap between two overall rates, that alone is no contradiction.
Let's gather it up.
A gap between gammas multiplies the odds, by the same amount for every patient.
What that does to a probability depends on where the patient starts.
And gammas depend on where zero is. Gaps do not.
One reminder: every gap we read today rests on 103 patients, so each one is rough. How rough is still to come.
And all this time, the lines have simply appeared, already in place.
Next time, we find out how the dial and the sliders settle where they do: fitting by balance.
This has been Model in Motion. Thanks for following the story.
